claims.text: This is a classic town Chinese diner built around wheat: ramen and chanpon egg noodles, gyoza wrappers, and shared woks and a single fryer used for fried chicken, gyoza, and fried rice. Cross-contamination with gluten is effectively unavoidable, so the kitchen is not celiac-safe.

Signature dishes such as the curry chanpon use thick wheat egg noodles, and the namesake Rokuhara-don is an ankake (thickened-sauce) bowl typically built on soy sauce and starch, so even the rice dishes are not safe for celiac diners.
The cold ramen is served in a vinegar-soy base and ankake dishes lean on soy sauce; standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) is brewed with wheat, so these sauces should be assumed to contain gluten.

The menu is centered on pork, chicken, egg, and seafood-based Chinese cooking with shared woks; even vegetable-forward dishes are cooked alongside meat and egg, so there is no documented vegan option and cross-contact is likely.

name: 六条新町 招福亭 (Rokujo Shinmachi Shofukutei)

claims.text: This is a soba/udon/donburi house and is not celiac-safe. Udon and the donburi (rice-bowl) sets are wheat-based, and the house green tea soba (chasoba) is a matcha-blended noodle that, like nearly all Japanese soba, is typically cut with wheat flour. Noodles are boiled in shared water, so cross-contamination is effectively unavoidable.

The broths are a sweet, dashi-forward Kyoto style built on soy sauce and fish dashi. Standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) contains wheat, so the broths should be assumed to contain gluten. No wheat-free soy sauce or tamari is indicated.

Not suitable for vegans. The dashi-based broths are made with fish stock, and the signature dishes feature egg, prawns, kamaboko (fish cake) and other animal products. There is no indication of a separate vegan broth or preparation.

name: 六曜社 地下店 (Rokuyosha Chikaten (Rokuyosha Basement S)

claims.text: This is a traditional kissaten whose signature item is a homemade wheat-flour donut made fresh on-site daily. Wheat baking and frying happen in a small shared space, so a strict celiac cannot be assured of a gluten-free experience here. Coffee itself is naturally gluten-free, but cross-contamination from the donuts cannot be ruled out.

The donuts and other sweets (pound cake, roll cake) are wheat- and dairy/egg-based baked goods, so they are not vegan. No vegan-specific menu is documented; black coffee with no milk would be the safest choice, but confirm directly.
Coffee is brewed plain, one cup at a time, and ordered black it contains no gluten ingredients.

This is a tonkatsu specialist: the core dish is pork coated in wheat flour and panko (wheat breadcrumbs) and deep-fried. The same shared oil is used for breaded items such as cream croquettes and potato croquettes, so the fryer is not gluten-free. There is no indication of any gluten-free or celiac-safe preparation.
No sources mention dedicated allergen handling, separate fryers, or gluten-free options. Anyone with celiac disease or a wheat allergy should avoid this restaurant.

Set meals come with miso soup (typically soy- and dashi-based) and the cutlets are served with a sweet house tonkatsu sauce, ponzu, or curry salt. Tonkatsu sauce and ponzu are generally wheat-containing, and Japanese miso soup commonly contains wheat-based soy sauce or dashi; none of these are documented as gluten-free here.

This is a pork cutlet specialist with no vegan or vegetarian menu indicated. The menu centers on deep-fried meat and seafood (pork cutlets, crab/shrimp cream croquettes), miso soup likely made with fish dashi, and shared frying oil, making it unsuitable for vegan diners.
No specific allergy-handling protocols or accommodations are mentioned in any available source. Diners with allergies should call the restaurant directly (075-393-2090) to confirm before visiting.

This is a town-Chinese noodle and gyoza shop. The core menu is wheat-based: chuka soba (ramen) and thin udon are wheat noodles, and the hand-made gyoza wrappers are wheat. Shared pots and surfaces mean heavy cross-contamination risk for anyone with celiac disease. Treat as not celiac-safe.

The broths and table condiments at a shop like this are soy-sauce based, and most Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) is brewed with wheat. The signature noodle bowls and gyoza dipping should be assumed to contain wheat-based soy sauce.

The broth is made from pork and chicken bones, and the noodle toppings include pork (chashu) and chicken, so the core dishes are not vegan and the kitchen handles meat throughout. No vegan options are indicated.

This is a retro coffee house whose food menu is built almost entirely on wheat: old-fashioned hot cakes (pancakes), toast and hot sandwiches, fruit sandwiches on castella-style bread, and Napolitan pasta. There is no documented gluten-free preparation, dedicated handling, or allergen protocol, so it is not celiac-safe and a celiac diner should avoid the food.

No reports describe separate equipment, surfaces, or cross-contamination controls for gluten. Drinks such as coffee and siphon-brewed coffee are inherently free of wheat ingredients, but no cross-contact assurances are documented.

No vegan options or dairy/egg-free preparations are documented. Signature items rely on butter, eggs, cheese, and house-made cream, and pancakes and breads are dairy- and egg-based, so a vegan diner cannot rely on suitable food here.
Everything is made in-house from scratch, so staff are likely to know exactly what goes into each dish if you ask directly about ingredients.

This is a miso-specialty restaurant, and miso is central to nearly every dish. Many Japanese miso varieties are made with wheat or barley koji, so the kitchen is heavily reliant on an ingredient that is frequently not gluten-free. Not celiac-safe.

The menu includes fried items such as miso-marinated fried chicken and shrimp-and-cheese rolls, plus a deep fryer in regular use; with no documented dedicated gluten-free fryer, fried foods carry cross-contamination risk.

The menu features 生麩 (nama-fu / fresh wheat gluten) dengaku, which is essentially pure wheat gluten and must be strictly avoided by celiac diners; its presence in the kitchen also raises broader cross-contact concern.

The food is built around miso (a soybean ferment) and the menu uses plum-miso, house 'name-miso,' and miso marinades throughout; combined with typical Japanese seasonings, gluten and soy exposure is heavy. Diners with soy allergy or wheat/gluten restriction should treat the menu as high-risk.
The oden dashi is animal-based. Sources describe it as a kombu-and-bonito (fish) combination or a chicken-bone-and-kombu stock, so the broth is not vegan even before the miso topping.

The signature oden and many dishes feature chicken (the giant chicken thigh, miso fried chicken), pork (white-miso braised pork belly), and seafood (clams in the cappuccino miso soup, shrimp rolls), so most plates are not vegan and vegetable items risk cross-contact with the shared animal-based dashi and pots.

There are a few naturally plant-leaning dishes on the menu, such as seasonal vegetables with house-made name-miso, that a vegan or vegetarian diner could ask about; given the miso focus, confirm with staff which items avoid the animal-based dashi.

name: 蕎麦 北山権兵衛 (Soba Kitayama-Gonbe)

claims.text: Not celiac-safe. The soba here is ni-hachi style — the kitchen states the noodles are roughly 80% buckwheat and 20% wheat flour, so wheat is a core ingredient of the soba itself.

Soba is boiled in shared pots and the kitchen also makes udon (pure wheat), tempura and rice bowls, so cross-contamination of any dish via shared boiling water, fryer oil and surfaces should be assumed.
Tempura items (tenzaru, kamaage, ten-namba) are wheat-battered and fried, adding wheat contact and likely shared fryer oil.

The dashi/tsuyu is soy-sauce based. Like most Japanese shoyu it almost certainly contains wheat, so the dipping and broth liquids should be treated as containing gluten. No wheat-free soy sauce or gluten-free tsuyu is mentioned anywhere on the restaurant's pages.
Not suitable for strict vegans. The house dashi is built from kombu and bonito (katsuo), so even vegetable-forward and broth-based dishes contain fish stock.
No vegan or plant-based options are listed, and the soy-based tsuyu is made with a bonito/kombu dashi base.
The kitchen openly publishes its soba ratio (about 80% buckwheat, 20% wheat) on its own menu page, which makes the wheat content transparent before you order.
The dashi is made from kombu and bonito without chemical seasonings, so the ingredients in the broth are relatively simple and identifiable.
